# typeset: a plain-text page layout tool

`typeset` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `target/debug/typeset`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `typeset`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage:

```
typeset [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] [--justify] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **40**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **14**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--justify`: justify the text (section 3). It takes no value.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"- "` (the character `-` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `* ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **cut**: whatever is on the current line is finished first, then the word is cut into pieces of exactly `n` characters, each piece on its own line, and the last piece (1 to `n` characters) is then treated like an ordinary word, so the following words may join it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `"| "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"* "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text of a level-1 heading is converted to upper case first, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `=` for level 1, `-` for level 2, none for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

**Justification** (only with `--justify`) applies to paragraphs, quotes and items, never to headings or figures. Every line of such a block except its **last** line is padded to the wrapping width of that block (page width, page width minus the quote prefix, page width minus 2): the single spaces between words are widened so that the line gets exactly that length. With `g` gaps and `d` characters to add, every gap gets `d / g` extra spaces (integer division) and the **leftmost** `d % g` gaps one more. Lines with a single word, and lines already at least as long as the width, are left as they are. The prefixes are added afterwards.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included), plus the lookahead below. If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Headings stay with what follows (keep with next).** The lookahead of a heading is: *nothing* if it is the last block or if a page break follows; all the lines of a following figure; for a following paragraph, quote or item, the first `min(L, ORPHANS)` lines of it, where `L` is the number of its lines (and ORPHANS the value in effect); for a following heading, all its lines plus one separator line plus *its* lookahead, recursively. The need of the heading is its own lines, plus one separator line, plus the lookahead (just its own lines when the lookahead is nothing). This is only a count of lines: it does not check that the following block could really be split there.
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

start.README.md:
# galley: a plain-text page layout tool

`galley` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `python3 src/galley.py` (entry point `src/galley.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). Usage:

```
galley [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **36**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **12**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **1**.
* There is no justification: `--justify` is an unknown option.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"* "` (the character `*` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `+ ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **kept whole**: it gets a line of its own (the line before it is finished first) which is simply longer than `n`; words after it start a new line, since nothing fits next to it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `"> "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"- "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `=` for level 1, `-` for level 2, `~` for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included), plus the lookahead below. If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Headings stay with what follows (keep with next).** The lookahead of a heading is: *nothing* if it is the last block or if a page break follows; all the lines of a following figure; for a following paragraph, quote or item, the first `min(L, ORPHANS)` lines of it, where `L` is the number of its lines (and ORPHANS the value in effect); for a following heading, all its lines plus one separator line plus *its* lookahead, recursively. The need of the heading is its own lines, plus one separator line, plus the lookahead (just its own lines when the lookahead is nothing). This is only a count of lines: it does not check that the following block could really be split there.
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

start.README.md:
# pagecraft: a plain-text page layout tool

`pagecraft` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `target/debug/pagecraft`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `pagecraft`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage:

```
pagecraft [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] [--justify] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **50**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **16**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **3**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--justify`: justify the text (section 3). It takes no value.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"+ "` (the character `+` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `* ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **cut**: whatever is on the current line is finished first, then the word is cut into pieces of exactly `n` characters, each piece on its own line, and the last piece (1 to `n` characters) is then treated like an ordinary word, so the following words may join it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 4 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `"  | "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"+ "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text of a level-1 heading is converted to upper case first, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `#` for level 1, `=` for level 2, none for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

**Justification** (only with `--justify`) applies to paragraphs, quotes and items, never to headings or figures. Every line of such a block except its **last** line is padded to the wrapping width of that block (page width, page width minus the quote prefix, page width minus 2): the single spaces between words are widened so that the line gets exactly that length. With `g` gaps and `d` characters to add, every gap gets `d / g` extra spaces (integer division) and the **leftmost** `d % g` gaps one more. Lines with a single word, and lines already at least as long as the width, are left as they are. The prefixes are added afterwards.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included). If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

## 6. Examples

`pagecraft --height 80 --width 50` reading this on standard input:

```
+ next surface figure ready river and
  cover. toward
+ word carry green young? warm interest gold table begin
#   Country



+ inch force told
  final short run fish full
+ day? appear let press own thing) rock south
  letter, final knew ten table shape a
+ Ran sea or, and deep
  yes
+ hard. eye machine out

> by can usual town game wood fast they how tree him state table fast



# Four tail! surface? eye girl;
# Noun be all plain miss.
```

prints:

```
+ next surface figure ready river and cover.
  toward
+ word carry green young? warm interest gold table
  begin

COUNTRY
#######

+ inch force told final short run fish full
+ day? appear let press own thing) rock south
  letter, final knew ten table shape a
+ Ran sea or, and deep yes
+ hard. eye machine out

  | by can usual town game wood fast they how tree
  | him state table fast

FOUR TAIL! SURFACE? EYE GIRL;
#############################

NOUN BE ALL PLAIN MISS.
#######################
-- 1/1 --
```

`pagecraft --height 7 --width 28` reading this on standard input:

```
were free never toward will wheel notice Dark soon beauty dog Tail street
able behind	

pose hot. map
vowel Able
produce  number run fill) is could in come. Than between
```

prints:

```

wheel notice Dark soon
beauty dog Tail street able
behind
-- 1/2 --

pose hot. map vowel Able
produce number run fill) is
could in come. Than between

```

```

```

```

```

and exits with status 1.

The visible examples (`tests/examples.json`, run with `python3 tests/run_examples.py`) use the same format as the hidden checks.

# folio: a plain-text page layout tool

`folio` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `target/debug/folio`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `folio`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage:

```
folio [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] [--justify] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **32**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **10**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **1**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **1**.
* `--justify`: justify the text (section 3). It takes no value.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"- "` (the character `-` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `* ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **kept whole**: it gets a line of its own (the line before it is finished first) which is simply longer than `n`; words after it start a new line, since nothing fits next to it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `": "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"- "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `=` for level 1, none for level 2, none for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

**Justification** (only with `--justify`) applies to paragraphs, quotes and items, never to headings or figures. Every line of such a block except its **last** line is padded to the wrapping width of that block (page width, page width minus the quote prefix, page width minus 2): the single spaces between words are widened so that the line gets exactly that length. With `g` gaps and `d` characters to add, every gap gets `d / g` extra spaces (integer division) and the **leftmost** `d % g` gaps one more. Lines with a single word, and lines already at least as long as the width, are left as they are. The prefixes are added afterwards.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included), plus the lookahead below. If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Headings stay with what follows (keep with next).** The lookahead of a heading is: *nothing* if it is the last block or if a page break follows; all the lines of a following figure; for a following paragraph, quote or item, the first `min(L, ORPHANS)` lines of it, where `L` is the number of its lines (and ORPHANS the value in effect); for a following heading, all its lines plus one separator line plus *its* lookahead, recursively. The need of the heading is its own lines, plus one separator line, plus the lookahead (just its own lines when the lookahead is nothing). This is only a count of lines: it does not check that the following block could really be split there.
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

## 6. Examples

`folio --width 20 --height 80` reading this on standard input:

```

electroencephalographically xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Real force
question! so Piece cover

will  took sing system field science pull
```

start.README.md:
# presswork: a plain-text page layout tool

`presswork` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `python3 src/presswork.py` (entry point `src/presswork.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). Usage:

```
presswork [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **44**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **18**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **3**.
* There is no justification: `--justify` is an unknown option.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"* "` (the character `*` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `+ ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **cut**: whatever is on the current line is finished first, then the word is cut into pieces of exactly `n` characters, each piece on its own line, and the last piece (1 to `n` characters) is then treated like an ordinary word, so the following words may join it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `"> "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"o "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text of a level-1 heading is converted to upper case first, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `-` for level 1, `-` for level 2, none for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included), plus the lookahead below. If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Headings stay with what follows (keep with next).** The lookahead of a heading is: *nothing* if it is the last block or if a page break follows; all the lines of a following figure; for a following paragraph, quote or item, the first `min(L, ORPHANS)` lines of it, where `L` is the number of its lines (and ORPHANS the value in effect); for a following heading, all its lines plus one separator line plus *its* lookahead, recursively. The need of the heading is its own lines, plus one separator line, plus the lookahead (just its own lines when the lookahead is nothing). This is only a count of lines: it does not check that the following block could really be split there.
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

## 6. Examples

`presswork --width 20 --height 80` reading this on standard input:

```

own
hot

should  main as Walk better with

do
class down list common wind mind her quick special fact between can laugh thing


foot find drive. found, base lay reach let lay pattern are still remember long there piece plain internationalization
```

# leadingd: a plain-text page layout tool

`leadingd` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `target/debug/leadingd`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `leadingd`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage:

```
leadingd [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] [--justify] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **28**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **12**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--justify`: justify the text (section 3). It takes no value.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"- "` (the character `-` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `* ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **cut**: whatever is on the current line is finished first, then the word is cut into pieces of exactly `n` characters, each piece on its own line, and the last piece (1 to `n` characters) is then treated like an ordinary word, so the following words may join it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `"| "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"- "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text of a level-1 heading is converted to upper case first, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `=` for level 1, `-` for level 2, `.` for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

**Justification** (only with `--justify`) applies to paragraphs, quotes and items, never to headings or figures. Every line of such a block except its **last** line is padded to the wrapping width of that block (page width, page width minus the quote prefix, page width minus 2): the single spaces between words are widened so that the line gets exactly that length. With `g` gaps and `d` characters to add, every gap gets `d / g` extra spaces (integer division) and the **leftmost** `d % g` gaps one more. Lines with a single word, and lines already at least as long as the width, are left as they are. The prefixes are added afterwards.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included), plus the lookahead below. If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Headings stay with what follows (keep with next).** The lookahead of a heading is: *nothing* if it is the last block or if a page break follows; all the lines of a following figure; for a following paragraph, quote or item, the first `min(L, ORPHANS)` lines of it, where `L` is the number of its lines (and ORPHANS the value in effect); for a following heading, all its lines plus one separator line plus *its* lookahead, recursively. The need of the heading is its own lines, plus one separator line, plus the lookahead (just its own lines when the lookahead is nothing). This is only a count of lines: it does not check that the following block could really be split there.
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

# lineset: a plain-text page layout tool

`lineset` reads a small markup document on standard input and lays it out on pages of a fixed width and height, like the typesetter of a line printer: blocks are wrapped into lines, lines are distributed over pages, every page gets a footer. Everything is counted in characters and lines (the input is ASCII), so the output is fully determined by the rules below.

Build and run it as `target/debug/lineset`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `lineset`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage:

```
lineset [--width N] [--height N] [--orphans N] [--widows N] < document
```

The pages go to standard output. The exit status is 0, or 1 if an `error:` line was printed (see sections 1 and 5).

## 1. Options

Options are read left to right, **before** the document is read.

* `--width N`: the page width in characters, 10 to 120; default **60**.
* `--height N`: the number of lines of a page, 4 to 80, footer not counted; default **20**.
* `--orphans N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the bottom of a page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* `--widows N`: the fewest lines of a split block allowed at the top of the next page, 1 to 4; default **2**.
* There is no justification: `--justify` is an unknown option.

A value is **1 to 3 ASCII digits** (leading zeros are fine: `040` is 40) that lies in the range of the option; if the same option is repeated the last value wins. The first problem found stops everything: the program prints one line and exits with status 1, without reading the document:

* `error: unknown option 'X'`: an argument that is not one of the options above (this includes plain words and forms such as `--width=30`);
* `error: missing value for --width`: the option is the last argument;
* `error: bad value 'X' for --width`: the argument after the option is not a valid value; it is taken as the value whatever it looks like (`--width --justify` is a bad value `'--justify'`), and the same message form (with the option name) is used for the other three options.

## 2. Reading the document

The input is split at newline characters; the lines are numbered from 1. Each line loses its **trailing white space** (spaces and tabs; white space always means space or tab, and *trimmed* means with white space removed at both ends). A line with nothing left is **blank**. A blank line only ends the paragraph, quote or item that is open (below) and is otherwise ignored; it does not count as a separator by itself (separators are decided in section 4).

Every other line is classified by the **first** rule that applies:

1. A line that is exactly `@break` is a **page break** block.
2. A line that *starts with* `@figure` must have the form `@figure NAME HEIGHT`: one or more spaces, a name of letters, digits, `_` and `-`, one or more spaces, a height of one or two digits that is at least 1, and nothing else; it is a **figure** block. Anything else is the error `bad figure` (section 5).
3. A line of one to three `#` followed by nothing or by a space and text is a **heading** block of that level (1 to 3); its text is what follows the `#`s, trimmed. A heading without text is the error `empty heading`. More than three `#`, or a `#` that is followed by another character (`#tag`), is not a heading.
4. A line starting with `>` is a line of a **quote**: drop the `>` and then one space if there is one; the rest, trimmed, is the quote text. If the open block is a quote, the text is appended to it (joined by one space); otherwise a new quote block starts.
5. A line starting with `"* "` (the character `*` and a space) starts a new **item** block; its text is the rest of the line, trimmed. Other bullet characters mean nothing here: a line starting with `+ ` is ordinary text.
6. If the open block is an item and the line starts with **two spaces**, its trimmed text is appended to the item (joined by one space): a continuation line.
7. If the open block is a paragraph, the trimmed line is appended to it (joined by one space), whatever its indentation.
8. Otherwise the trimmed line starts a new **paragraph** block.

The *open block* is the paragraph, quote or item that the previous non-blank rule line created or extended; it is closed by a blank line, by a break, figure or heading, and by a line that starts a different kind of block (so a paragraph line right after a quote starts a new paragraph, and an item line right after a paragraph starts an item, neither needing a blank line). Two item lines in a row make two items (rule 5 always starts a new item).

An item is **joined** when its first line comes directly after (the first line or a continuation line of) the previous item, with no line in between. Joined items form a tight list, see section 4.

## 3. Turning blocks into lines

The text of a block is a list of *words* (separated by white space). **Wrapping** to a width `n` is greedy: put words on a line, separated by single spaces, as long as the line stays at most `n` characters; the next word starts a new line. A word longer than `n` is **kept whole**: it gets a line of its own (the line before it is finished first) which is simply longer than `n`; words after it start a new line, since nothing fits next to it. Text without words wraps to one empty line.

* **Paragraph**: wrapped to the page width.
* **Quote**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); every line gets the prefix `"# "`.
* **Item**: wrapped to the page width minus 2 (at least 1); the first line gets the prefix `"* "`, every other line two spaces.
* **Heading**: the text, wrapped to the page width. Below the heading lines comes an **underline** line made of the underline character repeated as often as the *longest heading line* is long; the characters are `=` for level 1, `-` for level 2, none for level 3 (no underline line at all for a level without one).
* **Figure**: the line `[figure NAME]` followed by HEIGHT-1 lines `[ ]`; HEIGHT lines in all.
* **Page break**: no lines.

No output line ends with a space (trailing spaces, for instance of the quote prefix on an empty quote line, are removed from every output line; this does not change how many lines there are).

## 4. Pages

A page holds at most `--height` lines (the footer is not counted). The blocks are placed in document order, on the current page, starting with an empty first page. **Separator**: a block placed on a page that already has lines is preceded by one empty line, except an item that is *joined* when the block placed just before it on this page was an item, which has no separator. On an empty page there is never a separator, so no page starts with an empty line. The separator takes part in every calculation below ("fits" always includes it).

* **Page break**: if the current page has lines, a new empty page starts. Otherwise nothing happens (also at the start of the document, and several breaks in a row count as one).
* **Figures and headings are never split.** A figure needs all its lines. A heading needs its lines (underline included). If the current page has lines and the need does not fit in the room that is left (height, minus the lines used, minus the separator), a new page starts first; the block is then placed. On an empty page it is always placed, even if it is taller than the page (the page is then longer than `--height`).
* **Paragraphs, quotes and items may be split between pages.** Let `n` be the number of lines of the block and `room` the number of lines left on the current page after the separator. If `n <= room` the block is placed whole. Otherwise look for the **largest** `k` with `1 <= k <= min(room, n-1)`, `k >= ORPHANS` and `n-k >= WIDOWS`: the first `k` lines are placed on the current page (after the separator), a new page starts, and the remaining `n-k` lines are handled in exactly the same way on the new page (they may be split again). If there is no such `k`: when the current page has lines, a new page starts and the block is handled again on the empty page (it loses its separator); when the current page is already empty, the page is filled with the first `--height` lines of the block, a new page starts and the rest is handled the same way (the rules cannot be met, the block is cut at the page end).
* After the last block, a trailing empty page (created by a final page break or by a split that ended exactly at a page end) is discarded, unless it is the only page. An empty document is one empty page.

**Output.** For each page, its lines, then the footer `-- N/M --` (`N` the page number from 1, `M` the number of pages), each line ending with a newline; an empty line separates a footer from the next page. So an empty document prints just `-- 1/1 --`.

## 5. Document errors

A document error prints exactly one line, `error: line N: MESSAGE`, nothing else (no pages), exit status 1. `N` is the line number in the input. The messages are `bad figure` and `empty heading` (section 2), and `figure NAME is taller than a page` (a figure whose HEIGHT is greater than the value of `--height` in effect; `N` is the line of the figure). The document is checked in two passes: first the whole document is read (the first line that is a `bad figure` or an `empty heading` is reported), and only if that succeeds the figures are checked against the page height, the first too tall figure in document order being reported.

## 6. Examples

`lineset --height 80` reading this on standard input:

